doc.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Faking tunes on jobs with his father and carting the bass
summary: Father took him on jobs at fifteen where he had to fake tunes; Moore talks about the bassist's lot, learning tunes off records, and borrowed basses.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Did you two end up playing together?

We did, yeah, which also had its flip side to it. My father was also very particular about the bass notes. And he would take me on jobs when I was about fifteen years old, and when I was just finding my way around on the instrument, and I had to go out and fake 30 or 40 tunes in an hour. And as you might expect, I played a lot of wrong notes, and he was not very understanding about it. He somehow thought that I should just know them by a kind of magic. And so that’s why I’m still in therapy, Monk, after all these years.
Well gee, faking tunes you don’t know on the bass, I mean that’s about as hard as you could get.

Well that’s a kind of a curse of the instrument though. I mean even though say at a party like this, you’ll go up and the horn players will call a tune, and if the piano player knows it, or the guitarist knows it, you’re going to play it. They’re not going to not play it if you say well gee I’m not sure about this. “Oh, you’ll hear it,” you know. And that’s kind of the nature of the instrument. And I tell my students that. You turn on the radio, or put on a Frank Sinatra record, and play along with it, and try to find the bass notes. Because that’s a lot of what the job is about. And you know, very rarely, unless it’s your own group, do you get to call the songs. So that’s one of the real challenges of being a bass player I think.
Along with carting your instrument around.
Well that’s the worst part of it. That’s definitely the worst part of it.
Do you ever go to places where they’ll provide a bass for you?

Oh I do that quite a bit. I just came off a tour of England and I happened to know the instrument I was going to use in advance, except for one, and that was a bass player whose bass was almost unplayable, so I sounded like that fifteen year old kid again. But you either pay for it by getting the instrument there, so then you’re comfortable on the bandstand, or you have it the easiest in getting there and then pay for it on the bandstand. So even if it’s somebody else’s instrument that’s good, it’s never set up exactly the way you want it. Oh, it’s a real problem. Now Bob Haggart for example is going to use my bass. He didn’t want to bring one, so he’ll be using mine. So it’s not set up, I’m sure, the way he would prefer it to be. But that’s what we do with bass players.
